metadata.title: KL Chinatown Food Walk (Petaling Street) : Lala Noodles, Tau Fu Fah, Char Siew Bao, Apam Balik
metadata.description:
We embarked on the Kuala Lumpur Chinatown Food Walk (Petaling Street) with our knowledgeable host, Siddoz from A Chef's Tour. A fellow foodie with a deep understanding of the city's food landscape, Siddoz guided us through a culinary journey filled with legendary eats.

Our first stop was Lai Foong La La Noodle, renowned for its rich, flavorful noodle soup made with fresh lala (clams). The combination of delicate noodles and succulent clams in a savory broth was simply irresistible. We paired the noodles with a cham—a delightful blend of coffee and tea—before indulging in a flaky siew bao (baked bun) filled with delicious BBQ pork.

Next, we visited Kim Soya Bean, a popular stall known for its silky smooth tau fu fah (soybean custard dessert) and refreshing soy milk. The tau fu fah, topped with plain or palm sugar syrup, was warm, wobbly, and subtly sweet, melting in our mouths with every spoonful. The soy milk, on the other hand, was the perfect refreshing drink. People had queued up for this treat, a testament to its popularity.

Our journey continued at Madam Tang Machi Popo, famous for its muah chee—a traditional snack made from glutinous rice flour coated with ground peanuts and sugar. This humble dish is soft, chewy, and deeply satisfying. The spirit of the place was palpable; the owner’s voice still echoes through the shop, a comforting reminder of her legacy, even though she’s no longer with us.

We then ventured into Madras Lane, a bustling lane lined with hawker stalls. Here, we indulged in yong tau foo and curry laksa. The former was fish paste stuffed tofu and fish balls in a clear seafood broth, delicate and light, while the curry laksa packed a punch with its rich, spicy coconut milk base and hearty toppings. This lane truly epitomizes the vibrant street food culture of Kuala Lumpur.

Our next stop was a hidden gem serving steamed barbecued pork bao. These buns, traditionally made, were soft and fluffy, with a savory-sweet filling of barbecued pork. We packed some for later and made our way to Nam Heong, where we savored their Hainanese-style chicken rice. The poached chicken was tender, with a smooth, silky texture, perfectly paired with fragrant rice cooked in chicken broth.

The food adventure continued at Auntie Yin Popiah, where we tried popiah, a Chinese spring roll filled with a variety of fresh, dried, and cooked ingredients such as red kidney bean paste, chili sauce, lettuce, fried tofu, crushed peanuts, jicama, carrots, and more. Each bite was a burst of textures and flavors.

From there, we walked to an apam balik stall run by an elderly gentleman. His playful demeanor and agility made the experience even more enjoyable. Apam balik, a type of turnover pancake, was crispy on the outside with a soft, fluffy center filled with sweet corn, crushed peanuts, and sugar. Alongside, we sampled some nyonya kuih, a fluffy rice pancake.

Our final stop was Happy Meal Bakery, where we indulged in a classic egg tart. The crust was buttery and flaky, while the egg custard was smooth and mildly sweet—a comforting end to our flavorful adventure. In conclusion, our Petaling Street food tour was an unforgettable journey through the rich culinary tapestry of Kuala Lumpur.
